title: Reshaping Risks of Compound Hydroclimatic Extremes Over the Tibetan Plateau
content:
Abstract

The escalating compound climate extremes have critically threatened the water security and socioeconomic resilience of the Tibetan Plateau (TP), Asia's alpine water tower. However, the dynamic cascading processes by which compound climate extremes propagate into hydrological extremes remain poorly understood. We investigated the dynamic evolution of compound hydroclimatic risks and potential influencing factors under diverse meteorological forcings over the TP for the period 1980–2023. Our results revealed pronounced asymmetry in the propagation of compound meteorological extremes into runoff extremes. The conditional probability of extremely low runoff under hot-dry conditions (0.57) was higher than that of extremely high runoff under hot-wet conditions (0.47). Temporally, however, propagation probabilities exhibited contrasting trends, increasing under hot-wet conditions (+0.065 decade−1) but decreasing under hot-dry conditions (−0.084 decade−1), with significant increases and decreases observed across 39% and 47% of the TP, respectively (p < 0.05). Attribution analyses demonstrated that this asymmetric evolution was closely associated with soil moisture trends, which exhibited positive associations with propagation probability trends under hot-wet conditions and negative associations under hot-dry conditions. These findings highlight the reshaping of compound hydroclimatic risk patterns across the TP under a warming and wetting climate, providing critical insights for regional water resource management and disaster mitigation.
